title: Superior Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Superior wells have a 150 ft median depth, 10 gpm median yield, and estimated completed-well costs of $13,500-$22,500.
h1: What Superior, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
Buying land or a home in Superior means looking beyond the house and checking the water source. Within five miles, Colorado Division of Water Resources records include 4,462 permitted wells, but only 385 report a pump yield and 97 report a static water level. The records still show useful local patterns: a 150-foot median well depth, a 10.0 gallons-per-minute median yield, and water typically measured 20 feet below ground.

Those figures describe nearby permits, not a guarantee for a particular parcel. Ground conditions, the aquifer, well construction, and the location of the borehole all matter. Superior sits in a Denver Basin sedimentary-bedrock setting, with many permits also identifying fractured bedrock.

sections.heading: Superior well depths vary sharply by ground and aquifer
sections.html:
The median permitted well near Superior is 150 feet, but the middle half runs from 28 to 300 feet. That wide spread matters when reviewing a drilling bid: a median-depth estimate is only a starting point, and a parcel-specific quote may need room for a substantially shallower or deeper hole. The 90th percentile is 520 feet, while the deepest record reaches 1,989 feet.

Depth records also show that shallow wells are common, with 45% under 100 feet. Another 27% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 22% between 300 and 600 feet, and 7% at 600 feet or more. Nearby Louisville, Paragon Estates, Eldorado Springs, Lafayette, Broomfield, and Westminster can provide useful comparison records, but they do not replace checking the immediate neighbors.

sections.heading: A Superior well often makes useful household flow
sections.html:
Among the local wells that report pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 7.0 and 14.0 gallons per minute. That is a workable production range for many household uses, but a yield test is more important than the neighborhood median when sizing a pump, pressure tank, or storage system.

The low-end risk is present but not dominant in the records. 3% of reported yields are under 1 gallon per minute, and 7% are between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. Most, 67%, fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 23% exceed 15 gallons per minute. Ask for the well construction report and the actual pumping test, not just a seller's verbal description.

sections.heading: Recorded water levels near Superior are relatively shallow
sections.html:
The reported static water level has a median of 20 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 10 to 44 feet. Static level is the resting depth to water, not the depth of the well and not necessarily the level while pumping. A shallow static level can reduce pumping lift, but it does not by itself prove that the well will produce adequately.

The decade series does not show a simple long-term decline. Median depth to water was 34 feet in the 1950s, 30 in the 1960s, 18 in the 1970s, 26 in the 1980s, 19 in the 2010s, and 12 in the 2020s. The measurements are sparse, with only 97 total static-level records, so treat the pattern as local historical context rather than a basin-wide forecast.

sections.heading: Permit history shows a busy, changing well area
sections.html:
Permit activity near Superior is concentrated in the 1990s, when 1,640 permits were issued. The records show 101 permits in the 1950s, 157 in the 1960s, 279 in the 1970s, 227 in the 1980s, 560 in the 2000s, 277 in the 2010s, and 197 in the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025.

The largest named record holder is Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 1,205 records, followed by Boyles Bros. Drilling Co. (Lensch, George E) with 427, and Waneka & Son Drilling (Waneka, Don) with 310. These are historical permit-record names, not endorsements or proof of current availability. Confirm licensing, insurance, scheduling, and the written scope directly before hiring a driller.

sections.heading: Budgeting a new Superior well
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $50-$70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 150-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $7,500-$10,500. That is not the complete water-system price.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $13,500-$22,500 at the median depth. The broad local depth range is why a low initial bid can be misleading: drilling farther, casing and grouting requirements, difficult access, water testing, and site-specific electrical or trench work can change the final amount. Get the bid to state what happens if the hole is dry or the yield is below the target.

sections.heading: Check water quality, low yield, and the building site
sections.html:
Environmental history deserves a real review before closing. Within about ten miles of Superior, the map includes 319 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 128 historic mine features, and 33 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. A mapped site is a reason to investigate, not proof that a particular well is contaminated. Test the water through a qualified laboratory and review nearby environmental records.

Low yield, a dry hole, and fractured-rock unpredictability remain possible even where nearby wells perform well. Confirm the permit status and intended use with Colorado DWR. Domestic or household use accounts for 36% of local permits, while monitoring accounts for 46%; the use listed on a nearby permit may not match a residence. Before building, also confirm septic setbacks, well-to-septic separation, access for a drill rig, casing and grout requirements, and the site's legal ability to support the planned home.

sections.heading: Do the well investigation before buying a Superior lot
sections.html:
Start with the state well permit, construction report, pump test, water-quality results, and service records for the property. Then compare the closest completed wells rather than relying on the overall five-mile summary. A 150-foot neighborhood median with a 28-to-300-foot middle half should be carried into both the budget and the drilling-risk discussion.

For a vacant lot, have a driller and septic professional review access, setbacks, likely borehole placement, and the proposed home plan before you waive contingencies. For an existing home, confirm that the pump, pressure system, storage, and electrical equipment match the reported yield. If the basin is over-appropriated, water rights and an augmentation plan may affect what a new exempt household-use well can legally do. Have the permit and intended use checked before construction starts.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Superior, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported depth within five miles of Superior is 150 feet. The middle half runs from 28 to 300 feet, so nearby wells vary substantially. About 45% are under 100 feet, while 7% reach 600 feet or more. Use the closest comparable wells for a drilling estimate, not the median alone.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Superior?
faq.a: The local model uses $50-$70 per foot. At the 150-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $7,500-$10,500. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $13,500-$22,500. Actual cost depends on depth, access, construction requirements, and whether the well meets the target yield.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce near Superior?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a 10.0 gallons-per-minute median, with the middle half from 7.0 to 14.0 gallons per minute. About 3% of reported yields are under 1 gallon per minute, and 67% are between 5 and 15. These figures are not a guarantee; request the property's pump test and production history.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Superior, Colorado?
faq.a: The well records do not establish that a particular water supply is safe. Within about ten miles, maps show 319 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 128 historic mine features, and 33 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the property's water through a qualified laboratory and investigate nearby environmental records before relying on it for drinking.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping near Superior?
faq.a: The reported decade medians do not show a simple steady decline. Depth to water was 34 feet in the 1950s and 12 feet in the 2020s, with intervening medians of 30, 18, 26, and 19 feet. Only 97 wells report static levels, so this is limited historical context rather than a basin-wide prediction for a specific property.
